title: Reading People
objectives: I can explain what ten words say about how a person thinks, speaks, and acts.
I can use context clues to choose the best word for a character.
I can use the suffixes -ful, -ive, -ous, -ent, and -al to understand describing words.
I can write about two people with different styles using precise words.
rationale: Character words are the entry point for sixth-grade literary analysis: students must name traits precisely, not just say 'nice' or 'mean'. The ten words split into how people decide (cautious, impulsive, reluctant, persistent), how they speak and judge (sincere, candid, tactful, skeptical), and how they notice and carry themselves (perceptive, humble). Five of the words end in common adjective suffixes, so the unit opens the year's word-part work. Every later unit that analyzes a character, speaker, or historical figure reuses these words.

words.def: Careful to avoid danger, mistakes, or trouble.
words.ex: The cautious hiker tested each rock before putting her weight on it.
words.ex2: Nadia was cautious about sharing her password, even with close friends.
words.nonExample: Running across a busy street without looking is not a cautious choice.

segs.m: full of; having the quality of

apps.academic: In science, a cautious conclusion says only what the data can support.
apps.spoken: I'm being cautious because I don't know the answer yet.
apps.writing: Use cautious to show a character who thinks about risk before acting.

cloze.s: The ___ driver slowed to a crawl when the road turned to ice.

cloze2.s: After falling through the ice once, Mika became much more ___ near frozen ponds.

misuse.s: The cautious climber ignored every warning sign and jumped onto the loose rocks.
misuse.why: A cautious person avoids danger; this climber ignores it.

visual.alt: A climber testing a handhold beside a warning sign.

words.frame: I am cautious when I ___ because ___.

words.def: Not eager to do something; hesitating because you do not want to.
words.ex: Omar was reluctant to try out for the play, so he stood at the back of the line.
words.ex2: The reluctant witness answered only after the judge asked a second time.
words.nonExample: A student who jumps up first to volunteer is not reluctant.

apps.academic: Historians describe leaders who were reluctant to go to war.
apps.spoken: I'm a little reluctant to say yes before I see the plan.
apps.writing: Reluctant shows a character's feelings without saying 'he didn't want to'.

cloze.s: Priya was ___ to dive into the cold lake, so she tested the water with one toe for a full minute.

cloze2.s: The ___ puppy dug in its paws and refused to step off the porch into the rain.

misuse.s: Tomas was reluctant to open his gift, so he tore off the paper in two seconds and shouted with joy.
misuse.why: Reluctant means hesitating; tearing the paper open quickly shows the opposite.

visual.alt: A dog planting its paws at a door while rain falls outside.

words.def: Honest and truly meant, not pretended.
words.ex: Her sincere thank-you note mentioned exactly what the gift had meant to her.
words.ex2: The coach's sincere apology made the team believe he had learned from his mistake.
words.nonExample: A smile that someone puts on only to get something is not sincere.

apps.academic: Evaluate whether a speaker seems sincere by checking if actions match words.
apps.spoken: I'm being sincere: I really liked your idea.
apps.writing: Use sincere for feelings or praise that a character truly means.

cloze.s: Jonah's ___ apology included what he did wrong and how he planned to fix it.

cloze2.s: Everyone could tell her praise was ___ because she mentioned details only a careful listener would notice.

misuse.s: He gave a sincere compliment, though he did not mean a word of it and only wanted a favor.
misuse.why: A sincere compliment is truly meant; this one is pretended.

visual.alt: A handwritten card being handed over with a handshake.

words.frame: I know a person is sincere when ___.

words.def: Acting suddenly on a feeling without thinking first.
words.ex: In an impulsive moment, Dario bought three pairs of sneakers he could not afford.
words.ex2: It was an impulsive decision, and by evening Jun wished he had waited a day.
words.nonExample: Planning a trip for months and checking every cost is the opposite of impulsive.

morph.note: The final e of impulse is dropped before -ive.

apps.academic: A character's impulsive choice often starts the conflict in a story.
apps.spoken: That was impulsive of me; I should have asked first.
apps.writing: Pair impulsive with a result to show cause and effect in a character's choice.

cloze.s: The ___ shopper grabbed the first jacket she saw and paid before checking the price.

cloze2.s: Lena called her brother's quick decision to quit the team ___ and asked him to sleep on it.

misuse.s: She made an impulsive choice after comparing prices for two weeks and asking three experts.
misuse.why: Impulsive means acting without thinking; weeks of comparison is careful thinking.

visual.alt: A shopper rushing out of a store with bags.

words.frame: An impulsive choice can lead to ___.

words.def: Quick to notice and understand things that are not obvious.
words.ex: The perceptive teacher noticed that the quiet student was struggling before anyone said a word.
words.ex2: Her perceptive question showed she had spotted a flaw in the experiment.
words.nonExample: Walking past a clue that everyone else can see is not perceptive.
words.rel: how people notice and carry themselves

apps.academic: A perceptive reader notices details that point to a theme.
apps.spoken: That's a perceptive point; I hadn't seen it that way.
apps.writing: Use perceptive to credit a character for noticing what others miss.

cloze.s: The ___ detective noticed that the muddy footprints stopped at the open window.

cloze2.s: Only the most ___ student in the room caught the tiny error in the map's scale.

misuse.s: A perceptive friend never noticed that you were upset, even when you were crying.
misuse.why: Perceptive means quick to notice; failing to notice crying is the opposite.

visual.alt: A magnifying glass over a set of footprints.

words.def: Honest and direct, even when the truth is not easy to hear.
words.ex: In a candid interview, the coach admitted the team had played badly.
words.ex2: Be candid with me: does this draft need more work?
words.nonExample: Hiding the truth to avoid an awkward moment is not being candid.

apps.academic: Primary sources like diaries can be candid in ways official reports are not.
apps.spoken: To be candid, I think the first plan was stronger.
apps.writing: Use candid to describe honest feedback or a revealing photograph.

cloze.s: The mechanic gave a ___ answer: the old car was not worth the cost of repair.

cloze2.s: She asked her mentor for ___ feedback, and he did not soften a single weakness in the essay.

misuse.s: He was candid about his plans, so he dodged every question and changed the subject.
misuse.why: A candid person answers honestly; dodging questions is the opposite.

visual.alt: A line from 'hiding the truth' to 'telling the truth plainly', with candid near the honest end.

words.frame: A candid answer is one that ___.

words.def: Careful to say difficult things in a way that does not hurt feelings.
words.ex: Maya's tactful comment praised the project's colors before suggesting a bigger title.
words.ex2: It is hard to be tactful when you are frustrated, but it keeps friendships safe.
words.nonExample: Telling a classmate their singing is terrible is not tactful.

segs.m: skill in dealing with people kindly

apps.academic: A tactful peer review names strengths first and then asks a question about the weak part.
apps.spoken: Let me say this in a tactful way.
apps.writing: Use tactful when a character chooses gentle words for a hard truth.

cloze.s: The ___ nurse explained the test results slowly, choosing each word with care.

cloze2.s: A ___ reply to a gift you dislike is to thank the giver for thinking of you.

misuse.s: The tactful speaker laughed at the audience's questions and called them silly.
misuse.why: A tactful person protects feelings; laughing at questions hurts them.

visual.alt: Two friends talking, one speaking gently.

words.frame: A tactful way to say "no" is ___.

words.def: Continuing to try, even when something is hard or takes a long time.
words.ex: The persistent student practiced the same math problem until she understood it.
words.ex2: Beaver families are persistent builders, repairing their dams after every storm.
words.nonExample: Giving up after one hard try is not being persistent.

apps.academic: Scientists are persistent: a single failed experiment leads to a new question.
apps.spoken: I was persistent, and it finally worked.
apps.writing: Use persistent to show effort across time in a character or a historical figure.

cloze.s: The ___ reporter called the office every morning for a month until the mayor agreed to an interview.

cloze2.s: Thanks to ___ practice, Ravi finally landed the skateboard trick after dozens of falls.

misuse.s: A persistent runner quits as soon as the hill gets steep.
misuse.why: A persistent person keeps going when it is hard.

visual.alt: A hiker still climbing a steep mountain trail.

words.def: Doubtful about whether something is true until you see good evidence.
words.ex: A skeptical scientist asks, 'What is your evidence?' before accepting a surprising claim.
words.ex2: Mara was skeptical of the ad's promise to double her phone's battery life overnight.
words.nonExample: Believing every post you see online without checking is not skeptical.

apps.academic: Skeptical readers check the source and the evidence before trusting a claim.
apps.spoken: I'm skeptical; can you show me where you found that?
apps.writing: Use skeptical to show a reasoned doubt, not a rude one.

cloze.s: The ___ judge asked for a second set of records before accepting the witness's story.

cloze2.s: Be ___ of any headline that promises a miracle cure without showing evidence.

misuse.s: She was skeptical of the news, so she believed it immediately and shared it with everyone.
misuse.why: A skeptical person doubts first and checks evidence; sharing at once is the opposite.

visual.alt: A reader squinting at a newspaper headline.

words.frame: I am skeptical of claims that ___ unless ___.

words.def: Not proud or boastful; aware that you have things left to learn.
words.ex: Even after winning the state championship, the humble swimmer thanked her coaches first.
words.ex2: A humble leader asks for advice and admits when someone else has a better idea.
words.nonExample: Bragging about every win is not humble.
words.rel: how people notice and carry themselves

apps.academic: Humble scientists report results that went against their own prediction.
apps.spoken: I'm still learning, so I'll try to stay humble.
apps.writing: Use humble to describe a person who succeeds without boasting.

cloze.s: Despite her fame, the ___ author still answered every letter from students.

cloze2.s: The ___ chef admitted that his grandmother's recipe was better than anything he had invented.

misuse.s: He was humble about his victory and bragged about it all week.
misuse.why: A humble person does not brag; bragging all week is the opposite.

visual.alt: A champion holding a trophy and thanking others.

passage.title: Lena's First Round
paras: When her teacher asked her to join the debate team, Lena was reluctant. Speaking in front of strangers made her stomach flip, and she had always been the cautious type, the student who read every instruction twice before answering a single question.

Her partner, Dario, was her opposite. He was impulsive, signing up for debate, chess club, and the school play in a single afternoon. "You think too much," he told her. "Just say what you believe." His advice sounded sincere, but Lena knew that rushing had never worked for her.

Before the first round, their coach, Ms. Okafor, pulled them aside. She was perceptive, and she had noticed that Lena's notes were the best in the room. "Lena, you are persistent when you prepare," she said. "Use that. Dario, you are quick, but slow down and listen."

In the round, the other team claimed that school should start an hour later. Dario wanted to call the claim ridiculous, but Lena touched his arm. Instead she was tactful: "That is an interesting idea, but the evidence you shared comes from only one school." The judges looked skeptical about the opposing numbers, too.

Afterward, one judge said, "To be candid, your argument was stronger because it stayed calm." Lena felt proud, but she stayed humble. She knew Dario's energy had gotten them started, and her preparation had kept them going.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "reluctant" most nearly means
qs.why: Lena's stomach flips at the idea of speaking to strangers, which shows she hesitates; she is not eager.

qs.q: Why does Ms. Okafor tell Dario to "slow down and listen"?
choices: She thinks his ideas are weak.
She wants him to quit the team.
She has noticed that he acts quickly without thinking first.
She is angry that he joined other clubs.
qs.why: She calls him quick and the text calls him impulsive; her advice targets that habit.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Lena was tactful?
choices: She touched Dario's arm and then challenged the claim by pointing to its evidence politely.
She felt proud after the round.
She joined the team because her teacher asked.
qs.why: Tactful means choosing words that do not hurt; Lena disagrees by naming a weakness gently.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Speaking in public is always frightening.
Teachers choose the wrong students for debate.
People with different strengths can help each other succeed.
Quick decisions are always better than careful ones.
qs.why: Lena's preparation and Dario's energy together explain the team's success.

constructed.prompt: Describe two characters in a story, one cautious and one impulsive. Use both words and show each trait with an action.
look: gives one concrete action for each trait
constructed.model: Ana is cautious: she checks the weather and packs a first-aid kit before every hike. Her brother is impulsive: he starts up the trail in sandals without a map.

constructed.prompt: A friend asks if their poem is good, but you see problems. Write what you would say, using candid and tactful, and explain your choice.
look: gives an honest and kind response
constructed.model: I would be candid but tactful: I would say the images are strong and ask whether the ending could be clearer. That way I tell the truth without hurting my friend.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for describing people and use them to analyze a character in a short narrative, practice the suffixes -ful, -ive, -ous, -ent, and -al, and write about contrasting styles.

notes.va.cautious.adj: Contrast with impulsive on a two-column chart. Students often confuse cautious with fearful: a cautious person may be brave but still plans.
notes.va.reluctant.adj: Reluctant is about feeling hesitant to act; it is not the same as lazy. Ask what a reluctant character does with her body.
notes.va.sincere.adj: Sincere is about whether feelings are truly meant. Have students judge two thank-you notes, one specific and one generic.
notes.va.impulsive.adj: Model the suffix: impulse + -ive. Ask students for an impulsive choice that turned out well, to show the word is not automatically negative.
notes.va.perceptive.adj: Distinguish from smart: a perceptive person notices. Use a 'what did you notice?' routine with a picture.
notes.va.candid.adj: Often confused with candy and with rude. Use the shades ladder: candid is honest and direct; tactful adds care for feelings.
notes.va.tactful.adj: Show -ful meaning 'full of'. Practice rewriting three blunt sentences tactfully.
notes.va.persistent.adj: Persist + -ent. Contrast with stubborn: persistence continues toward a goal; stubbornness refuses to change a mind.
notes.va.skeptical.adj: Skeptical is a reasoned doubt, not a rude one. Link to the 'what is your evidence?' routine in science and argument units.
notes.va.humble.adj: Humble does not mean having low self-worth. A humble person can be proud of work while crediting others.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The text says Lena read every instruction twice. That is a careful habit, so I would call her cautious. Dario signs up for three things in one afternoon without planning, so impulsive fits him. I can prove each word with an action from the text.'
discuss: Which character in a book you know is perceptive? What did they notice?
How can a person be both persistent and humble?

teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit cautious/impulsive and candid/tactful as opposite pairs two days later, again at one week, and use them in discussion of any character in the next unit.
